intro: Emo Court's great yew is 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall, a many-stemmed tree in the parkland south-east of the house. A yew at Emo was measured in 1794 by Samuel Hayes for his Practical Treatise on Trees; whether it was this one, nobody can prove. The national register gives it 200 to 300 years as of 2009, so somewhere between 200 and 400 today. The gardens and parkland are run by the Office of Public Works and open all year in daylight.
meta_description: The Emo Court yew in Co. Laois: 4.37 metres round, many-stemmed, perhaps the yew measured here in 1794. Parkland open all year in daylight.
question_meta: Emo's oldest tree is the many-stemmed yew in the Emo Court parkland, aged somewhere between 200 and 400 years.
question_answer: Emo's oldest mapped tree is the European Yew (Taxus baccata) in the parkland of Emo Court, 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall in 2009. Its age is estimated at somewhere between 200 and 400 years.
question_context: The Tree Register of Ireland measured the yew in August 2009 and listed it as number 54. The national heritage tree register recorded one yew at Emo on the same day, in coppice form, and gave it 200 to 300 years. Both records very probably describe the same tree, though neither says so. Samuel Hayes measured a yew at Emo in 1794 and included it in his Practical Treatise on Trees. The Ancient Yew Group asks whether this is that tree and leaves the question open. If it is, the yew was already worth measuring more than 230 years ago. In 2009 the yew measured 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall, which put it in the Tree Register's ancient class. It grows as a coppice, many stems rising from one base. Counting the years since 2009, the register's band comes out at roughly 200 to 300 years or a little more. Emo Court is managed by the Office of Public Works, and Laois County Council says the gardens and parkland are open all year in daylight.

trees.name: The Emo Court Yew

trees.story:
In 1794 Samuel Hayes measured a yew at Emo and put it in his Practical Treatise on Trees, among the good yews of his day. Whether it was this one, nobody can prove. The Ancient Yew Group, which keeps the record, asks the question and leaves it open, and so do we.

What is certain is the tree itself. When the Tree Register of Ireland visited in August 2009 it measured 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall, which put it in the register's ancient class. The national heritage tree register, on the same day, recorded one yew at Emo in coppice form, many stems rising from one base, and gave it 200 to 300 years. The two records almost certainly describe the same tree, since it was the only yew either team wrote down here, but they never say so in as many words.

Add the years since and the age comes out at somewhere between 200 and 400. If the 1794 yew is this one, it was already a tree worth measuring more than 230 years ago. Nothing dates it further back than that.

Emo Court is managed by the Office of Public Works, and Laois County Council says the gardens and parkland are open all year in daylight. The house is a separate guided tour. Check heritageireland.ie before you set out, since seasonal hours vary.

official_register.name: Tree Register of Ireland (no. 54) via Ancient Yew Group record 5160

trees.access: Emo Court gardens and parkland, managed by the OPW: Laois County Council says open all year during daylight hours; UCC Tree Explorers lists seasonal opening times. The house is a separate guided tour. Check heritageireland.ie before going.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its many stems rising from one very wide base, nearly four and a half metres round. It is the dark yew standing in the parkland south-east of the house.
trees.verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group (recording the Tree Register of Ireland, visit 1 Aug 2009): the Emo Court yew is number 54 on the Tree Register's site, height 14 m, girth 4.37 m, 'ancient' class 4-5 m. They note it was measured by Samuel Hayes in 1794 and appears in his 'Practical Treatise on Trees' (Hayes's 'good yews'): the group asks whether this is one of those but does not claim it, so only 'a yew at Emo was measured in 1794 and the register's yew may be it' can be said. Heritage Trees of Ireland (Tree Council / A. Fennell, 1 Aug 2009, same day) holds one Taxus baccata at Emo, record 624, 'coppice', age band 200-300 years at 2009; pin 53.10553,-7.19212 is its Irish Grid conversion (about 100 m), so the match with the register tree is probable, not proved (same date, only yew recorded). Age is a derived range: register band 200-300 plus 17 years, Hayes 1794 mention would imply 230+ years; nothing dates it beyond that, so 200-400 stays broad. Laois County Council's own page mentions a 'yew walk' ending at the Ceres statue near the house; whether this is the tree in the walk is not stated. Alive: no recent dated photo of THIS tree; lifecheck RECENT 2024-08-18 within the estate (iNaturalist), register is 2009 and records no vitality. Recognition line candidate: a very wide, multi-stemmed ('coppice' form) dark yew standing in the parkland south-east of the house, girth of nearly four and a half metres. Pin is register-level only. Register-only for the tree itself, owner OPW publishes the garden but not this tree: flagged.
